---
title: "Research"
subtitle: "Heat, sleep and physiological strain in free-living populations"
---

My research asks a deceptively simple question: **how much heat is too much, and
for whom?** Answering it means measuring people where they actually live and
sleep, modelling exposure–response relationships that are rarely linear, and
then turning those relationships into thresholds that a public health agency
can act on.

Three strands run through the work — field measurement, statistical modelling,
and evidence synthesis — and most projects use all three.

---

## Project HEATS — Heat Exposure, Activity and Sleep {#heats}

[Analytical lead · NRF CREATE programme · 2025–present]{.eyebrow}

Project HEATS characterises the indoor thermal environment of Singapore homes
and dormitories and links it to objectively measured sleep. I lead the
statistical analysis and manuscript development for the heat exposure
workstream.

**Design.** Wearable and in-home monitoring across three field waves
(Jun 2025 – Jul 2026): bedroom temperature, humidity, CO₂ and particulates
alongside actigraphy-derived sleep outcomes. The primary analysis covers
**122 participants and 10,303 person-nights**.

**Methods.** Linear mixed-effects models with **Mundlak within/between
decomposition**, which lets us separate what a person does in response to a hot
night (behavioural adaptation) from what heat does to them (physiological
strain) — a distinction that a single pooled coefficient hides. Non-linear
threshold work uses piecewise and segmented models with AIC-based knot search
and restricted cubic splines, comparing dry-bulb temperature against composite
indices (wet-bulb temperature, Heat Index) as predictors of sleep disruption.

**Outputs.** A protocol paper under review at *BMC Public Health*; the primary
sleep-continuity analysis in preparation; three oral presentations at Indoor Air
2026; a 30-night field trial of a dynamic "down-rise" bedroom cooling profile.

::: {.note-box}
Findings from this programme were covered nationally in *The Straits Times* and
*Lianhe Zaobao* in June 2026, and cited by the Chairman of the National Research
Foundation Singapore.
:::

## Exertional Heat Vulnerability Index (eHVI) {#ehvi}

[Evidence-synthesis lead · protocol lead and guarantor · NRF & NEA, CISR-2024-2R-04]{.eyebrow}

A Climate Impact Science Research programme building a heat vulnerability index
for Singapore. I lead the evidence-synthesis workstream: I developed the
systematic review protocol underpinning the index — search strategy, extraction
framework and synthesis approach — and serve as guarantor of the review. I also
chair the bi-weekly technical review and act as quality gate for the report
blocks delivered to the funder.

Registered as PROSPERO **CRD420261289729**.

---

## Cooling Singapore 2.0 {#cs20}

[Analytical lead, physiological workstream · NRF]{.eyebrow}

Controlled laboratory heat-exposure studies across population groups who are
usually treated as a single "general public" in advisory design: children,
heat-unacclimatised adults and older adults. I model the physiological and
perceptual responses and translate them into policy-relevant insight for
tailoring national heat-health advisories — the point being that one threshold
for everyone protects nobody particularly well.

---

## Evidence synthesis {#reviews}

Four PROSPERO-registered reviews, two of which I lead and two of which I
supervise. Together they map what is actually known about nighttime heat and
about the tools used to warn people.

| Registration | Review | My role |
|---|---|---|
| **CRD420261289729** | Heat vulnerability index development in urban settings | Lead author, protocol lead, guarantor |
| **CRD420251052384** | Heat health advisory tools and their effectiveness (113 studies) | Lead author |
| **CRD420251009764** | Adverse nighttime heat thresholds and effects on sleep, comfort and health (177 records) | Second author, supervisor |
| **CRD420251134107** | Fluid temperature and form in cooling (60 studies, 644 participants) | Second author, supervisor |

Methodologically this work follows PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-P, with MMAT and
Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 appraisal, multilevel sensitivity models, publication
bias assessment and certainty-of-evidence grading.

## Behaviour, nutrition and health {#nutrition}

My doctoral and postdoctoral work addressed a parallel question in a different
domain: what determines what people actually eat, and which of those
determinants can be moved?

- **Team sport athletes** (PhD, TUS Athlone) — dietary intake against sports
  nutrition guidelines, nutrition knowledge, and cooking and food skills, using
  a mixed-methods design to identify modifiable behavioural targets.
- **UK households in the cost-of-living crisis** (King's College London) —
  cooking and food behaviours, food insecurity, diet quality and mental
  wellbeing, combining hierarchical regression on large survey datasets with
  thematic analysis of focus group and open-text data.

The methodological thread — behaviour is a modifiable exposure, and you have to
measure it well before you can change it — is the same one that runs through the
heat work.

## Applied and advisory work {#advisory}

**External reviewer, Sport Singapore** — SEA Games 2025 heat resilience pilot.
With A/Prof Jason Kai Wei Lee and Dr Pearl Tan, I serve on the NUS external
review panel for an athlete questionnaire (*n* = 68) and in-competition core
temperature profiling across five sports, with ongoing input to the national
heat resilience roadmap.

**Peer review** — *Sports Medicine – Open*; *Environmental Science and Pollution
Research International*; *Journal of Science in Sport and Exercise*; *Journal of
the International Society of Sports Nutrition*.
